name: Haworth
frame_note: mosaic centre as printed in LPSC 2024 #1775 Table 1; frame not named in source (LRO-based, MOON_ME assumed); representative point, not a NASA-defined centre

potential.text: NASA states that each of its 13 candidate regions of 2022, this one included, contains sites with continuous access to sunlight throughout a 6.5-day period, useful for solar power on a short surface stay; those sites lie somewhere in the roughly 15 × 15 km region and are not necessarily this representative point, so sunlight here must be computed for the exact point and dates.

NASA chose its 13 candidate regions of 2022, this one included, so that landing sites lie close enough to permanently shadowed regions for a crew moonwalk, an opportunity to sample cold traps; which shadowed area, how far it is from this point and whether it holds ice are not stated, and our PSR maps are not loaded yet.

NASA reports that prior studies found signs of ice in permanently shadowed areas within Haworth crater, after which this region is named, a possible target for ice prospecting; the evidence is indirect, gives no amount or depth, and the distance from this point to those areas has not been computed.

LROC describes the Malapert massif as thought to be a remnant of the South Pole-Aitken basin rim, so its rocks could help date that ancient impact; the origin is an interpretation, and no sampling target at this point has been assessed.

LROC places the heart of the Malapert landing region on a relatively flat area near 86°S, 0°E that continues down the slope toward the Earth; whether this point gets more Earth line of sight than other sites must come from the validated station calculation, not from the slope's orientation.

No site-specific ice or hydrogen measurement for this point is in our sources yet (LRO Diviner and LEND data not loaded), so local water ice is unknown; permanent shadow nearby, where present, would not prove ice.

name: Shackleton Rim Site04
label: NASA reference point on the inner crater wall (31.8° slope), not a landing site
frame_note: frame not stated in source (coordinates generated from the PGDA LOLA DEM files, Data Book A2.1); MOON_ME assumed - Leo to verify
source_label: NASA Lunar Surface Data Book, table A2-2 (p. 58); centre point of a DEM polygon, not a point picked on the terrain (section A2.1, p. 57)

potential.text: LROC reports three points on Shackleton's rim that are collectively sunlit for more than 90% of the year, which makes this area attractive for solar power; that figure belongs to those three rim points together, not to this reference point, whose sunlight must be computed for its exact position and dates.

Shackleton's interior is in permanent shadow, a cold trap where frozen volatiles could be studied; permanent shadow is a thermal condition, not proof of ice, and access from this point has not been assessed.

NASA states that Shackleton's permanently shadowed interior is believed to contain ice, which would make it a high-value sampling target; this is an expectation, not a measured deposit, and its amount and depth are unknown.

name: Connecting Ridge
label: Blue Moon MK1 target
frame_note: mosaic centre as printed in LPSC 2024 #1775 Table 1; frame not named in source; this point is not Blue Moon MK1's landing point, which is not published

potential.text: LROC reports that the elevated ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters has portions illuminated up to 90% of the time, though nowhere permanently, which favours long solar-power windows; the best-lit portions are not necessarily at this mosaic-centre point, so its sunlight must be computed for the exact point and dates.

NASA states that each of its 13 candidate regions of 2022, this one included, contains sites with continuous access to sunlight throughout a 6.5-day period, useful for solar power on a short surface stay; those sites lie somewhere in the roughly 15 × 15 km region and are not necessarily this representative point, so sunlight here must be computed for the exact point and dates.

LROC marks a relatively flat area on the Shackleton-de Gerlache ridge with a direct line of sight onto the floor of Shackleton crater, which has been in perpetual shadow, an opportunity to observe a cold trap; this is not evidence of ice, and that flat area is not necessarily this point.

No site-specific ice or hydrogen measurement for this point is in our sources yet (LRO Diviner and LEND data not loaded), so local water ice is unknown; permanent shadow nearby, where present, would not prove ice.

name: IM-2 Athena intended site
label: intended landing site, not touchdown
frame_note: intended site as quoted by LROC (26 Feb 2025); frame not stated (MOON_ME assumed); actual touchdown 84.7906 S 29.1957 E (LROC image 1408); NASA: more than 400 m from the intended site
source_label: LROC featured image 1401, IM-2 Landing Region

potential.text: LROC notes that Mons Mouton, where this intended site lies, is thought to have formed as part of the South Pole-Aitken basin rim, which makes it of keen scientific interest; that origin is an interpretation, not a sampled result.

IM-2 carried instruments to investigate Mons Mouton, but the lander came to rest on its side more than 400 m from this intended site and could not fully operate its drill, so no local ice measurement exists and ice here remains unknown.

name: VIPER Mons Mouton
label: cancelled 2024; delivery re-awarded 2025, site not confirmed
frame_note: Beyer et al. 2025 Appendix B: Moon (2015) sphere, planetocentric, east-positive, R = 1737.4 km (datum named in source; MOON_ME equivalence not verified)
source_label: Beyer et al. 2025, VIPER Site Analysis, PSJ 6, 236

potential.text: Beyer et al. describe the VIPER mission area as containing accessible permanent shadows in craters of varying ages, giving a rover nearby cold traps to sample; 'accessible' is that mission analysis's judgement, and permanent shadow is not proof of ice.

Chandrayaan-1 M3 data suggest one possible surface water-ice detection in the extended VIPER mission area, in a permanently shaded spot with annual maximum temperatures below 110 K, a concrete target for verification; it is a single tentative orbital detection, and ShadowCam images of the area's shadowed craters show no surface-exposed ice or frost.
Radar-derived rock proxies suggest Mons Mouton is unusually rock-poor, which could ease landing and driving; rock distributions vary locally, so each site still needs image-based hazard checks.
